subtype: Approach: mixing two ideas into one plan [Thinking]
passage: When I, Nirmala, was in Class 6, my group in Dumdum had a fight over the science exhibit. Two of us wanted a clay model of a volcano, and two of us were sure a big poster would win the prize. We argued for two days, Disha. Then Meenal, the quietest one, said, "Why not both?" We made a poster showing how volcanoes form, with a little model that moved in the middle. The modellers glued the clay, the drawers coloured the poster, and both sides got the part they cared for. We came second in the exhibition, and nobody sulked at all.

qa.q: How long did the group in Dumdum argue?
qa.a: The group argued for two days.

qa.q: What did Meenal want, and how might Meenal have felt, when saying, "Why not both?"
qa.a: Meenal was probably tired of the two-day argument and hopeful that a plan keeping both ideas would end it without either side losing.

qa.q: What choice inside the story ended the argument, and why did it work?
qa.a: The choice to make a poster with a small model worked because both sides kept the part they cared about.

qa.q: How did Meenal's idea look to the two sides who had been arguing?
qa.a: Both sides could see their own idea in the plan, so nobody felt they had lost; the result was that nobody sulked.

grounding: Two children want a model and two want a poster, and the group combines them into one plan so each keeps the part they care about.
